cards.title: Define the offer before choosing a mechanic
cards.summary: An offer is the total proposition before purchase—positioning, price architecture, value mechanic, risk reversal and urgency—not just a discount, and picking mechanics starts by defining all five variables together.
cards.use_when: Planning a promotion or rebuilding a product page proposition and unsure whether to cut price or change something else
steps: Write the offer as five variables: (1) product positioning — who it is for and what job it does; (2) price architecture — entry price, bundle price, tier ladder; (3) value mechanic — bundle, gift, threshold, subscription or discount; (4) risk reversal — guarantee, returns, trial; (5) urgency — real deadline or quantity limit.
Treat straight discounting as only one of the five offer mechanics, alongside product repositioning, bundles, gift with purchase, and tiered threshold offers.
Choose the mechanic that fits the margin problem: if the constraint is contribution margin, prefer repositioning, bundling, gift or threshold over cutting price.
Make the same offer statement congruent across ad, landing page, checkout and email, and remove any expired promotion from every surface.
Write down the margin math before launching (new break-even ROAS, target CPA, expected UPT lift), so you can judge whether the offer is worth running.
caveats: The five-variable framing is the source's model; other offer frameworks exist, but this one forces margin and risk reversal into the same decision.
Congruence across ad, page, checkout and email is stated as a baseline requirement — mismatched or expired offers are treated as a broken offer, not a creative issue.

cards.title: Five non-discount offer mechanics to protect margin
cards.summary: Product repositioning, bundles, gift with purchase and tiered threshold offers all raise units or value per transaction without the exponential ROAS pressure of price cuts.
cards.use_when: Conversion is acceptable but margin is thin, or you need a promotion that does not train customers to wait for sales
steps: Product repositioning: change the frame — bundle for a named occasion, reframe the hero SKU for a specific customer job, or sell the outcome rather than the product. This changes perceived value without changing price.
Bundles: combine complementary SKUs into one purchasable unit so AOV rises and per-unit shipping and fulfillment cost falls, which helps contribution margin even at the same unit prices.
Gift with purchase: add a low-cost, high-perceived-value item tied to a threshold or SKU, keeping headline price intact while lifting perceived value and UPT.
Tiered threshold offers: set spend thresholds that unlock progressively better value, using them to pull buyers up to the next tier instead of discounting every order.

Disciplined straight discounting: reserve it for cases with a clear margin plan, since it compresses gross margin and raises the ROAS required to hold contribution profit. Verify current platform discount-link and threshold mechanics when building.
caveats: For each mechanic, run the margin math — an offer that raises conversion but kills profit is not a good offer.
Gift with purchase and threshold offers need a real cost of goods on the gift; a free high-cost gift can lose money faster than a small discount.

cards.title: Margin math of discount depth: required ROAS grows non-linearly
cards.summary: Flat discounting compresses gross margin so the ROAS needed to hold the same contribution profit increases exponentially as the discount deepens, even though units per transaction typically rise.
cards.use_when: Deciding discount depth, or judging whether a proposed sale price can still fund paid acquisition
steps: Calculate pre-discount contribution profit per order: revenue minus COGS minus variable costs.
Apply the discount to revenue and re-subtract the same COGS and variable costs. Note that per-order profit falls faster than price because cost of goods does not discount.
Compute the new break-even ROAS: 1 divided by the new contribution margin percentage (contribution profit divided by revenue). Compare it with the old break-even ROAS to see the required lift.
Estimate the UPT or conversion lift the discount is expected to produce — UPT typically increases after a discount, which partially offsets the margin loss.
Recalculate target CPA at the discounted margin so the paid team is not spending against an outdated efficiency target.
Only proceed if the UPT or conversion lift can realistically cover the higher required ROAS; if not, switch to a non-discount mechanic.
caveats: The source treats discount-driven UPT lift as typical but not guaranteed; the size of the lift is an assumption you should test, not a fixed benchmark.
Verify current channel attribution and ROAS definitions in your ad platform before comparing break-even ROAS targets.

cards.title: Upsell rules: one per slot, relevancy over price, measured in margin
cards.summary: Upsells work when limited to one offer per slot, relevant to the item being bought, high-margin, easy to understand, and measured by gross margin lift rather than take rate alone.
cards.use_when: Designing in-cart, checkout or post-purchase add-ons and deciding what to show in each slot
steps: Show one offer per slot — stacking multiple upsells in the same placement splits attention and reduces take rate on each.
Prioritize relevance over price: suggest an accessory or consumable that fits the product already chosen, not the cheapest item in the catalog.
Favor high-margin SKUs as the upsell, since the incremental revenue converts to profit at that SKU's margin rate.
Keep the offer easy to understand: one clear product, one clear price, one clear benefit.
Measure each upsell by incremental contribution profit, using take rate x AOV lift x gross margin %, not take rate alone.
Kill any upsell with a strong take rate but weak margin lift, and look for margin-first alternatives in the same slot.
caveats: A take rate on its own can mislead: a low-margin add-on with a high take rate may contribute less than a smaller number of high-margin upgrades.
The gross-margin-lift formula is the source's measurement method; it requires knowing true COGS and variable cost per upsell SKU.

cards.title: Match upsell friction to cart stage: post-purchase anchor, checkout add-ons
cards.summary: High-friction full-product upsells belong post-purchase where attention is free, while checkout is best used for low-friction add-ons like shipping protection; use post-purchase as an anchor with a down-sell path.
cards.use_when: Choosing where in the funnel to place a cross-sell or upsell and how much decision weight to ask of the buyer
steps: Map the stages: in-cart, checkout, and post-purchase. Each has different attention and abandonment risk.
At checkout, place only low-friction add-ons — shipping protection, expedited delivery, small warranties — that require a one-click decision and cannot derail checkout.
Post-purchase, anchor with the highest-value relevant offer, then down-sell to a lower-priced option if the first is declined. Attention is highest and cart risk is zero at this stage.
Avoid adding full products as checkout upsells if they make the buyer reconsider the order; the abandonment risk outweighs the take-rate gain.
Track take rate and incremental contribution profit separately by placement so you learn which stage actually earns margin.
Verify current post-purchase and checkout app behavior in your platform, since one-click add-on flows and post-purchase offers change by provider.
caveats: Placement is a trade-off: post-purchase reduces risk of cart abandonment but reaches only buyers who complete checkout.
The source's conclusion that low-friction add-ons outperform full products at checkout is a design principle, not a measured law — test on your own catalog.

cards.title: Set thresholds on the binomial AOV distribution, not the mean
cards.summary: Threshold offers miss because they are set above average order value; the binomial AOV distribution shows the peaks where real order values cluster, so tiers should be anchored to those peaks.
cards.use_when: Choosing free-shipping thresholds, tier cut-offs, or gift-with-purchase spend levels
steps: Pull a sample of real order values, not just the reported mean AOV.
Plot order values as a distribution rather than reading a single summary number. The source describes the shape as binomial, with visible peaks at common order values.
Identify the peaks — often at a single hero SKU price or a natural two-item combination — and set thresholds just above the next peak to pull buyers up one cluster.
Avoid setting a threshold between peaks, where few orders sit: buyers will either not qualify or will have to add an awkward amount.
Re-run the distribution after any price, bundle or threshold change, since moving a price moves the peaks.
Check that each threshold still clears margin after the gift or shipping cost is included.
caveats: The binomial description is the source's way of saying orders cluster; the exact shape depends on your catalog and price points.
A threshold offer requires cost math — free shipping or a gift at a threshold can be unprofitable on low-margin carts.

cards.title: Score an upsell by incremental contribution profit
cards.summary: Use take rate x AOV lift x gross margin percentage to compare upsells on profit, not on how often they are accepted.
cards.use_when: Comparing two candidate upsells, or deciding whether to keep an existing add-on
steps: Calculate take rate: the share of eligible buyers who accept the offer.
Calculate AOV lift: the difference in average order value between exposed and non-exposed or self-selected groups, accounting for buyers who would have bought the add-on anyway.
Multiply by the gross margin percentage of the upsell SKU to get incremental contribution profit per eligible buyer.
Compare candidates on this number rather than on take rate; a high-take-rate, low-margin item can rank below a lower-take-rate, high-margin one.
Re-measure margin after COGS changes, since a supplier price increase can flip which upsell wins.
If the source of the AOV lift is unclear, run a holdout rather than inferring lift from exposed-buyer averages.
caveats: Treating take rate as the KPI is the common failure mode the source warns about; take rate is an input to the profit formula, not the goal.
The formula needs defensible AOV lift and gross margin inputs — self-selected upsell acceptance overstates incremental lift.

cards.title: Embed subscription unlocks into the primary offer
cards.summary: Make subscription part of the main proposition — a lifetime discount or an unlock tied to joining — rather than a separate loyalty pitch after purchase, to drive retention from the first order.
cards.use_when: Launching or redesigning a consumable product's purchase flow and deciding how subscription is presented
steps: Decide what subscribing unlocks versus what one-time buyers get — the source describes embedding a lifetime discount or an unlock into the primary offer.
Present subscribe-and-save on the product page and in the buy box as a first-class choice, not a checkbox buried at checkout.
Make the subscriber benefit permanent and legible ('lifetime' pricing) rather than a first-order-only promotion, so the reason to stay subscribed survives order one.
Keep the one-time purchase path available and honest; forced subscription creates cancellations and refunds that erode the retention gain.
Measure subscriber retention and lifetime value against the margin given up in the subscription discount, and check the math still clears contribution profit.
Verify current subscription platform mechanics — dunning, pause, skip and cancellation flows — in your specific provider.
caveats: A lifetime discount is a permanent margin concession; it only pays if retention and repeat rate actually improve, which should be measured rather than assumed.
Subscription structure is best suited to consumables with predictable repeat cycles; the source's guidance assumes repeat purchase.

input.text:
03-OFF / offers

Goes here. The proposition before purchase. Offer mechanics, guarantees and risk reversal, bundles, discount depth against margin, subscription structure, upsells, price anchoring, referral programs with tracked economics. Specifically capturing the definition of an offer vs a discount, the five core offer mechanics (product repositioning, bundles, gift with purchase, tiered offers, straight discounting), cross-sell/upsell structuring, and the margin math underlying discount economics.

Not here.

A gift in the box after purchase -> 17-CXP

A one-off giveaway engineered for UGC, not repeatable -> 19-WLD

The price of the product itself -> 01-PRD

Paid social campaign account structure -> 11-ADC

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Deconstructs the margin economics of discounting (showing how required ROAS grows exponentially) and provides five specific non-discount offer mechanics to preserve gross margin while increasing units per transaction.

modules: [OFF]

topics: [offer mechanics, bundles and AOV, discount depth and margin, upsell take rates, subscription structure]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. offer mechanics / the five variables of an offer (product positioning, price architecture, value mechanic, risk reversal, urgency) vs a flat discount. The five offer mechanics: product repositioning, bundles, gift with purchase, tiered threshold offers, and disciplined straight discounting. discount depth and margin / how flat discounting compresses gross margin, showing that target ROAS to maintain contribution profit increases exponentially as the discount deepens. upsell take rates / cross-sells vs upsells, friction levels at different cart stages (in-cart, checkout, post-purchase), and optimizing for incremental contribution profit rather than just take rate. bundles and AOV / using the binomial average order value (AOV) distribution to set correct threshold targets rather than relying on the mean AOV. subscription structure / embedding subscription unlocks and lifetime discounts into the primary offer to drive retention.

Look for. The margin math behind discounting: calculating the new break-even ROAS and Target CPA after factoring in a discount, acknowledging that Units Per Transaction (UPT) typically increases. The formula for calculating incremental contribution profit on upsells: Take Rate % * AOV Lift * Gross Margin %. The five rules of upselling in cart: 1 offer per slot, relevancy over price, focus on high-margin SKUs, easy to understand, and measured by gross margin lift. The correct placement of upsells: anchoring high post-purchase and down-selling, and using low-friction add-ons (like shipping protection) at checkout instead of full products. Setting threshold offers based on the peaks of a binomial AOV distribution curve, rather than the average AOV.

Skip. General advice on running a 52-week promo calendar. The "Hierarchy of Influences" framework comparing budgets, account structures, and creative. Offer advice with no margin math. An offer that raises conversion and kills profit is not a good offer, and a source that ignores this is not worth ingesting.

Scope mix. Mostly growth. The baseline is congruence: ad, page, checkout and email state the same offer, and no expired promotion is visible.

Volume. 20 to 30.
